aiSummary: Speckled trout are the standout species across Choctawhatchee Bay right now, actively feeding bay-wide, with bull redfish also showing well — including a recent 40-inch, 26-lb bull red reported near Santa Rosa Beach. Water is 86°F and slightly stained under cloudy skies, with a waning crescent moon driving a strong tidal push that should concentrate fish on moving water. Work the morning tide window hard; a 29% storm chance after 1 PM makes an early start and a plan to wrap up or retreat to protected water by early afternoon the smart play.

bridge.aiNote: The 331 Bridge spans the narrow neck of Choctawhatchee Bay, creating a current funnel where bait gets pushed through on both tides. Pilings hold trout, redfish, sheepshead, and black drum year-round, with the lee-side pilings serving as the prime ambush zone on incoming tides. This open-water spot is the first on the bay to become unfishable when wind picks up or weather builds.
bridge.todaysCall: The low tide falls around 2:42 PM — fish the morning hours while the tide is still pulling, as the spring-tide tidal push with a waning crescent moon will funnel bait through the bridge and put fish on the bite. SE winds at 0–10 mph are light enough to keep conditions fishable at the pilings early, but that favorable window closes as the storm chance ramps up after 1 PM. Work the lee-side pilings with soft plastics or live shrimp; slightly stained water means fish will be holding tight to structure rather than roaming. Target trout and reds in the moving current, and plan to clear this exposed, open-water location well before the afternoon storm window opens.

alaqua.aiNote: Alaqua Bayou offers protected water with a strong year-round redfish population, along with trout and flounder at the mouth. The oyster bars at the creek mouth are the prime target, and tree cover keeps temperatures a few degrees cooler than the open bay while providing shelter from wind and weather. The upper creek transitions toward brackish water and can hold bass alongside smaller reds.
alaqua.todaysCall: Alaqua is a strong call today — the tree cover and protected nature of the bayou make it one of the better places to be on a hot, stormy-risk August day with a heat index up to 102°F. Work the oyster bars at the creek mouth as the tide falls toward the 2:42 PM low; the spring-tide tidal movement will push bait off the bars and concentrate reds and trout in predictable ambush positions. Slightly stained water favors darker soft plastics or noisy lures like a popping cork with live shrimp to help fish locate the bait. With storms possible after 1 PM, plan to be fishing by early morning and use the protected interior as your fallback if weather builds.

basin.aiNote: Basin Bayou sees less fishing pressure than nearby Alaqua and LaGrange, meaning the fish here tend to be less educated and more willing to bite. The interior grass flats are classic sight-fishing territory for redfish in less than two feet of water, and pompano occasionally appear at the mouth on moving tides in late spring and early summer. It offers less weather protection than LaGrange when conditions deteriorate.
basin.todaysCall: The combination of light pressure and a strong tidal push from the spring tide makes Basin Bayou worth a morning visit — reds on the interior grass flats in skinny water are catchable early before the sun gets high and the heat index climbs past 100°F. Slightly stained water will limit sight-fishing quality compared to a clear-water day, so lean on a popping cork with shrimp or a weedless soft plastic worked slowly over the grass edges rather than pure sight-casting. The falling tide toward the 2:42 PM low should push bait toward the mouth, setting up a productive window mid-morning. Given that Basin offers less weather protection than LaGrange, keep a close eye on the sky and be ready to run for cover well before the post-1 PM storm window.

lagrange.aiNote: LaGrange Bayou is the top trout producer among the bayous in this area, with legendary oyster bars at the mouth and interior grass flats that hold redfish year-round. Deep holes inside the bayou hold black drum and sheepshead, adding variety to the lineup. It is also the most protected water on the north side of the bay, making it the go-to location when weather threatens.
lagrange.todaysCall: LaGrange is the top pick today — it combines the best trout and redfish habitat in the area with the most weather protection available, which matters given the 29% storm chance after 1 PM. Hit the oyster bars at the mouth early as the tide is still moving, letting the strong spring-tide push concentrate trout and reds on the upcurrent edge of the structure. The bay-wide bite report confirms speckled trout are actively feeding across Choctawhatchee Bay right now, and LaGrange's oyster bars are among the most reliable addresses for those fish. Slightly stained water favors a chartreuse or white soft plastic under a popping cork, or live shrimp tight to the oyster edges. If afternoon storms fire up, simply move deeper into the bayou — the protected interior holes can hold black drum and sheepshead and keep you fishing safely.

fourmile.aiNote: Four Mile Creek is a tidal creek running between Shipyard Marina and the bay, where tidal flow pushes baitfish up the creek on incoming tides and concentrates redfish and trout in the bends and along grass edges. The upper section transitions toward brackish water and holds bass alongside smaller reds, while the creek mouth is a reliable flounder zone. Short and well-protected, it is the safest fishery on this part of the bay when weather threatens.
fourmile.todaysCall: Four Mile Creek is an excellent insurance play today — it is the most protected option near the 331 Bridge, which matters with afternoon storms possible after 1 PM. The tidal flow will be falling toward the 2:42 PM low, so focus on the inside bends and grass edges where reds and trout stack up as bait gets pushed out of the creek on the ebb. A weedless soft plastic or shrimp under a float worked through the tighter inside bends should be the first approach in slightly stained water. The creek mouth is worth a few casts for flounder as the tide falls and pushes bait to the edge. If storms develop early, this creek gives you the ability to stay tucked in and keep fishing safely.

hogtown.aiNote: Hogtown Bayou is a signature Santa Rosa Beach guide spot and one of the most productive trout flats on the bay, with summer mornings being the peak time as trout stack on grass in two to four feet of water. Spanish mackerel appear at the mouth on moving tides. It sits further from the 331 Bridge than the other bayous, so factor in the longer run time when planning your day.
hogtown.todaysCall: The bay-wide bite report specifically calls out Hogtown Bayou flats as a concentration point for redfish this time of year, and the active trout bite across the bay makes this a compelling destination if you're willing to make the run from the north side. Get there early — summer mornings are peak on these grass flats, and the combination of cloudy skies and slightly stained water will keep fish comfortable in the shallows longer than on a clear, sunny day. The spring-tide tidal movement will be your friend; work a topwater or popping cork over the two-to-four-foot grass zone during the morning moving water before the tide bottoms out at 2:42 PM. The longer run time is the main logistical concern today — leave enough margin to be back off open water before the post-1 PM storm window, and watch the western sky carefully once you're out there.

mallet.aiNote: Mallet Bayou is a small tributary that feeds directly into LaGrange Bayou just south of Freeport, and its direct connection to that top-producing system means LaGrange's oyster-bar trout-and-redfish pattern plausibly extends into this quieter, less-pressured water. There is far less documented fishing history for Mallet Bayou compared to LaGrange itself, so approach it with realistic expectations. Its small, interior character makes it a calm-water fallback when wind picks up on the open bay.
mallet.todaysCall: Mallet Bayou is best fished today as a complement to a LaGrange trip rather than a standalone destination — slip in here if LaGrange's most pressured spots have boats on them or if you want to work quieter water with potentially less-wary fish. The falling tide toward the 2:42 PM low should move bait out of the interior, and the same trout-and-redfish pattern that makes LaGrange productive likely applies here given the direct connection. Keep presentations simple: a soft plastic on a light jig head or live shrimp worked along any visible grass or oyster edge. The small, protected interior is a genuine asset today given the storm risk after 1 PM — you can stay tucked in safely while waiting to see what the weather does.

mack.aiNote: Mack Bayou sits on the barrier-island side of Choctawhatchee Bay near Topsail Hill Preserve State Park, well west of the 331 Bridge — making it a long-run destination rather than a quick local trip. It shares the same protected-bayou character as Alaqua and LaGrange, with marsh grass, oyster bars, and a few interior holes, and sees less pressure simply due to its distance from the main boat ramps. Hewett Bayou and Buck Bayou sit immediately to the east and are realistically fishable on the same trip.
mack.todaysCall: Mack Bayou rewards anglers willing to make the run with lighter pressure and fish that see fewer lures — a real advantage when targeting trout and reds in 86°F, slightly stained water. The spring-tide tidal movement should push bait through the oyster bars and grass edges at the mouth; time your arrival to fish the morning falling tide before it bottoms out at 2:42 PM. The biggest concern today is the run itself — the open bay crossing takes time, and with a 29% storm chance after 1 PM, you need to budget for a safe return window. Leave early, fish the morning hard, and plan to begin your return trip well before noon. If time allows, Hewett and Buck Bayous next door let you extend the trip without retracing water.

hewett.aiNote: Hewett Bayou sits immediately east of Mack Bayou on the barrier-island side of Choctawhatchee Bay near Topsail Hill Preserve State Park, sharing the same protected-bayou habitat of oyster bars, marsh grass, and a few deeper interior holes. Light pressure due to its distance from main boat ramps keeps the fish here less conditioned to lures than spots closer to Freeport. It pairs naturally with Mack and Buck Bayou as part of a single trip to this side of the bay.
hewett.todaysCall: Hewett Bayou is best approached as part of a Mack-Hewett-Buck Bayou run on the 30-A side rather than a solo destination — the long crossing from the north side demands you make the most of the trip by fishing multiple stops. Oyster bar edges and grass mouths are the focus; the falling tide into the 2:42 PM low will push bait to predictable ambush points for trout and reds. Slightly stained water makes a noisy presentation like a popping cork with shrimp or a paddle-tail swimbait a better call than a finesse approach. The same storm-window caution applies here as with Mack Bayou — this is a long run from shelter, so keep a vigilant eye on the western sky and be on your way back to protected water long before the post-1 PM storm risk materializes.

buck.aiNote: Buck Bayou is the smallest and least-documented of the three neighboring bayous on the barrier-island side of Choctawhatchee Bay near Topsail Hill Preserve State Park. Its habitat should track its larger neighbors — marsh grass, some oyster structure, and a modest interior — but there is less basis to speak confidently about what it consistently produces. It is best treated as a bonus stop on a Mack and Hewett Bayou trip rather than a standalone destination.
buck.todaysCall: Fish Buck Bayou as the last stop on a 30-A bayou run after working Mack and Hewett — it is small enough to explore in a short amount of time and adds variety without requiring a separate trip. If the oyster and grass structure at the mouth resembles its neighbors, the falling morning tide and spring-tide push could set up a brief but productive window for trout and reds before the low at 2:42 PM. Keep expectations calibrated: limited fishing history means fewer guarantees here, so spend no more time than the morning window allows before turning toward home. With the long return run and storms possible after 1 PM, Buck Bayou should be your last cast of the morning, not the reason you stay out too long.
